title: HDFS and MapReduce: the ideas that survived
goal: By the end you can trace a MapReduce job through map, partition, shuffle and reduce, say when a combiner is safe and what it saves, and point at where each of these ideas lives on in Spark.

warmup.q: Three machines each hold part of an authorization log. To count each word, the system runs 3 counting tasks that produce the final totals (MapReduce calls them reducers). The word `approved` appears on all 3 machines. How many of the counting tasks end up counting `approved`?
options: All 3, and a final step adds their answers together
Exactly 1, picked by hashing the word
Whichever counting task is free first
None: each map task counts its own words and the totals are merged at the end
warmup.why: Every map task sends a key to the reducer that `hash(key) mod 3` picks, and the hash of `approved` is the same on every machine. So every machine sends its `approved` counts to the same counting task, which can total them alone. That's why no final merge step is needed.

sections.h: HDFS cuts files into big blocks and stores each one three times
sections.body:
In 2004 a typical machine in Google's MapReduce cluster had two 160 GB disks. A 1 TB web crawl doesn't fit on it, and lesson 1 showed you wouldn't want it to: one disk needs hours to read a terabyte. So the data has to live on many machines at once. Build that storage the way lesson 1 built the scan, from the simplest version up.

Version 1: put each file on one machine. A 400 MB settlement file goes on machine 7. This breaks twice. A file bigger than one machine's disks can't be stored at all. And when machine 7 dies, the file is gone.

Version 2: cut every file into fixed-size pieces called **blocks**, and spread the blocks over many machines. Now a file can be bigger than any disk, and many machines can read one file at the same time. But a program that wants the file now needs to know where its blocks are. So one server keeps that list: for each file, its blocks, and for each block, the machines that hold it. Data about data like this is called metadata.

Version 3: keep copies. Machines still die, and their blocks die with them, so store every block on three machines. When one dies, the other two still serve the block, and the system makes a new third copy somewhere else. Keeping several copies is called replication.

That's the design of the Google File System (GFS, published in 2003), and of HDFS, the Hadoop Distributed File System. Hadoop is the open-source project that rebuilt Google's GFS and MapReduce designs. In HDFS the machines that store blocks are DataNodes, and each block is a plain file on a DataNode's local disk. The metadata server is the NameNode. Blocks are 128 MB by default (`dfs.blocksize`; GFS used 64 MB) and stored three times (`dfs.replication`). A client asks the NameNode where a file's blocks are, then streams the bytes straight from the DataNodes. File data never flows through the NameNode.

Why such big blocks? A 400 MB file is only 4 blocks, so the NameNode keeps 4 entries for it and can hold the metadata for millions of files in memory, as the GFS master did. And each read becomes one long sequential stream, which is what disks do well.

The copies are placed on purpose. Machines sit in racks, cabinets of machines that share a network switch and power, so one broken switch can cut off a whole rack. When a DataNode writes a file, HDFS puts the first copy on that machine and the other two on two machines in one other rack. A dead disk, machine or rack loses no data.

Block locations had one more use. In 2004 the network was the scarce resource. The paper's machines had 100 Mb/s or 1 Gb/s links, and the network as a whole carried far less than all the machines' disks could read at once. So the scheduler ran each piece of work on a machine that already held a copy of its block. The data stayed put and the code travelled to it. This is **data locality**.

Cutting input into big pieces with one piece of work each is still how Spark reads files. Spark is the engine most of this track uses: it runs one job across many cores or machines. It cuts each input file into input partitions of at most 128 MB, set by `spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes`, and runs one task per partition.

try.title: Watch Spark cut a file into tasks
steps: From the `labs` folder, run `SplitsDemo`. The first run writes a 300 MB log file to `bigdata/build/l02/` (a few seconds).
Predict first: how many input partitions does Spark make from 300 MB with 128 MB splits? And with 32 MB splits?
Compare with the output. One partition is one task, the way one HDFS block was one map task.

code.title: SplitsDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
file: auth-log.txt, 300 MB
maxPartitionBytes=128m -> 3 partitions, so 3 map tasks
maxPartitionBytes=32m  -> 9 partitions, so 9 map tasks
```

`128m` means 128 MiB, 134,217,728 bytes. 300 MB is 2.2 of those, so Spark makes 3 splits; with 32 MiB it makes 9. The demo runs Spark with 2 cores on purpose. With many cores and a small file, Spark shrinks the splits so every core gets work, though never below `spark.sql.files.openCostInBytes` (4 MB). So on a bigger machine you may see more partitions than the 128 MB rule suggests.

sections.h: Map, shuffle, reduce, one key at a time
sections.body:
Now compute something over those blocks. Take the question the trace demo below answers: how many times does each status (`approved`, `declined`, `refunded`) appear in an authorization log spread over three machines? Build the computation the same way, from the simplest version.

Version 1: every machine sends every status it reads to one machine, which counts. That is correct, and it falls over at scale. Change the question to "how many payments per card" over a billion cards. The counting machine now receives the whole input through one network link: 1 TB through a 1 Gb/s link (125 MB/s) takes over two hours. And it must keep a counter for each of the billion cards in memory, on a machine with 2 to 4 GB.

Version 2: use R counting machines and give each one a share of the keys. A key is whatever you group by: a status, a card number, a merchant. For this to work, every machine that sends data must send a given key to the same counting machine, without asking anyone. A hash function gives exactly that. Java's `String.hashCode()` turns a string into a number, and the same string gives the same number on every machine. Take that number modulo R (the remainder after dividing by R) and you get a machine number from 0 to R minus 1. Hadoop's rule is `(key.hashCode() & Integer.MAX_VALUE) % R`. The `&` clears the sign bit, so the result is never negative.

Version 3: a counting machine now receives values for many keys, from many machines, in no useful order. If it sorts them by key first, equal keys sit next to each other. Then it can finish one key, write its result, and move on to the next, holding only one key's values in memory at a time.

That is MapReduce, published by Jeff Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat of Google in 2004. You write two functions. Map takes one input record and emits key/value pairs: the line `approved declined approved` becomes `(approved, 1)`, `(declined, 1)`, `(approved, 1)`. Reduce takes one key with all of its values and emits a result: `approved` with `[1, 1, 1, 1, 1]` becomes `approved = 5`. A master program splits the input, runs one map task per block on a machine that holds it, and runs R reduce tasks, called reducers. Everything between map and reduce is called the **shuffle**:

1. Each map task splits its output into R parts with the partitioning function, and writes the parts to its own machine's local disk.
2. Each reduce task fetches its part from every map task over the network.
3. Each reduce task sorts what it fetched by key, calls reduce once per key, and writes one output file to the distributed file system: `part-00000`, `part-00001`, and so on.

Because a key always hashes to the same reducer, one reducer sees every `approved` in the whole input, and reducers never need to talk to each other.

Failures are handled by running tasks again. The master pings every worker. When a worker dies, its map tasks run again on another machine that holds a copy of the block. Even the map tasks that had finished run again, because their output sat on the dead machine's local disk. Finished reduce tasks don't run again: their output is already in the replicated file system. This only works because map and reduce are deterministic: run them twice on the same input and you get the same pairs.

steps: Run `MapReduceTraceDemo`. It runs the stepper's job and prints each phase.

map C:    (declined,1)->r0 (approved,1)->r1 (refunded,1)->r2

Every `approved` is tagged `r1`, on all three nodes, because `String.hashCode()` gives the same number everywhere. All nine pairs cross the shuffle. Each record costs its key (8 bytes here) plus 4 bytes for the count.

refs.title: MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters (Dean and Ghemawat, OSDI 2004)

sections.body:
Go back to version 1 for a moment and make it smarter: let each machine count its own block first, and send totals instead of single pairs. A map task that read a million events would send five numbers for five statuses instead of a million pairs. That trick, applied before the shuffle, is a **combiner**: it runs the reduce logic on one map task's output before anything crosses the network.

It matters because every pair a map task emits costs disk space, network time and sort time. In a payment log most pairs are `(approved, 1)`. The MapReduce paper points out that word frequencies follow a Zipf distribution: a few words are very common and most are rare. So each map task emits thousands of copies of the same few pairs. With a combiner, map task A turns `(approved, 1), (approved, 1)` into `(approved, 2)`. The reducer still adds everything up. It just receives fewer, bigger numbers. In Hadoop the combiner is often the reducer class itself.

This is only correct when the operation gives the same answer however you group and order the pieces. Sum passes: (1 + 1) + 3, 1 + (1 + 3) and 3 + 1 + 1 are all 5. So do count, min and max. Mathematicians call this being associative and commutative. Average fails. Say map task 1 sees two payments for a merchant, 1,000 and 3,000 cents, and averages them to 2,000. Task 2 sees one payment of 10,000. The average of the two averages is 6,000, but the true average of the three payments is 4,667. Combine `(sum, count)` pairs instead, and divide once at the end. The worked example below does exactly that.

A combiner also needs repeated keys to pay off. If the key is a payment id or an idempotency key, each key appears once per map task, and the combiner saves nothing.

try.title: Turn on the combiner
steps: Run the trace again with `-Pargs=combine` (command below). Compare the map lines and the `shuffled` line with the previous run.
Read the two `count by` lines at the end. They run the same arithmetic on 20 map tasks of 50,000 events each.
Predict before you look: which key gains more from a combiner, `status` or `payment id`?
try.expect:
```text
map A:    (approved,2)->r1 (declined,1)->r0
map B:    (approved,2)->r1 (refunded,1)->r2
map C:    (declined,1)->r0 (approved,1)->r1 (refunded,1)->r2
reduce 0 gets: (declined,1) (declined,1)
reduce 1 gets: (approved,2) (approved,2) (approved,1)
reduce 2 gets: (refunded,1) (refunded,1)
shuffled: 7 records, 84 bytes
output:   declined=2, approved=5, refunded=2
count by status      without combiner: 1,000,000 records 12,000,000 bytes   with:       100 records      1,200 bytes
count by payment id  without combiner: 1,000,000 records 15,000,000 bytes   with: 1,000,000 records 15,000,000 bytes
```

Same output, fewer records. On the tiny input the combiner saves 2 records out of 9. With 5 statuses and 50,000 events per task, it sends 100 records instead of a million. With payment ids it saves nothing, because no key repeats inside a task.

sections.h: Why MapReduce lost, and what survived
sections.body:
MapReduce wrote everything to disk on purpose. Map output went to local disk, and every job's final output went to HDFS, three copies. That made failures cheap to recover from, and it made pipelines slow. Real work is rarely one job. A daily settlement report built from five chained jobs wrote its intermediate data to HDFS, three copies, and read it back, five times over. Machine learning was worse: an algorithm that passes over the same data 20 times ran as 20 jobs, each reading the whole input from HDFS again.

Spark's answer came from the RDD paper (Resilient Distributed Datasets, NSDI 2012): keep intermediate data in memory between steps. When a machine dies, Spark recomputes the lost pieces from their **lineage**, the recorded chain of steps that produced them, instead of keeping three copies of every intermediate result.

Hadoop clusters faded after that. The 2021 Lakehouse paper notes that from 2015 on, cloud object stores (S3, ADLS and GCS: services that keep files as named objects and serve them over HTTP) started replacing HDFS. They are cheaper and someone else runs them. Today Hadoop survives mostly as client libraries inside Spark, such as the S3A connector that lets Spark read S3. Don't start a new project by writing MapReduce jobs.

The ideas did survive, nearly all of them:

| MapReduce idea | Where it lives now |
|---|---|
| Big blocks, one task per block | Spark input partitions, 128 MB by default |
| Move the code to the data | Read fewer bytes: partition pruning and pushdown (lessons 3 and 4) |
| hash(key) mod R | Spark's `Exchange hashpartitioning(...)`, and Kafka's key to partition rule |
| The combiner | A partial aggregate before the shuffle (`partial_count`) |
| Map output on local disk | Spark's shuffle files, still written to local disk |
| Re-run a deterministic task | Spark recomputing lost partitions from lineage |
| One output file per reducer | The `part-00000` files in every Spark output folder |

The local-disk row matters most. "Spark runs in memory, so it never touches disk" is wrong: Spark's own guide says a shuffle "generates a large number of intermediate files on disk". Lesson 6 of this track is all about the shuffle.

try.title: Find MapReduce inside a Spark plan
steps: Run `SparkWordCountDemo`. It counts the same three lines with Spark's DataFrame API, a table-like dataset you transform with calls such as `groupBy`. Before the result it prints the physical plan: the tree of steps Spark decided to run.
Read the plan from the bottom up, like data flowing upward. Find the map side, the combiner, the shuffle and the reduce.
What is R, the number of reducers, in this plan? The demo's session sets `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` to 4.

code.title: SparkWordCountDemo.kt
code.src:
package sfz.bigdata.l02.demo

import org.apache.spark.sql.Encoders
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.explode
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.split

/** The same three-line word count in Spark, with the physical plan Spark chose for it. */
fun main() {
    val spark = demoSpark()
    val lines = spark.createDataset(
        listOf("approved declined approved", "approved refunded approved", "declined approved refunded"),
        Encoders.STRING(),
    )
    val counts = lines
        .select(explode(split(col("value"), " ")).alias("word"))   // map: one row per word
        .groupBy("word")                                           // shuffle by word
        .count()                                                   // reduce (and combine)
    counts.explain()
    counts.orderBy("word").show()
    spark.stop()
}

try.expect:
```text
== Physical Plan ==
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
+- HashAggregate(keys=[word#6], functions=[count(1)])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(word#6, 4), ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS, [plan_id=15]
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[word#6], functions=[partial_count(1)])
         +- Generate explode(split(value#1,  , -1)), false, [word#6]
            +- LocalTableScan [value#1]

+--------+-----+
|    word|count|
+--------+-----+
|approved|    5|
|declined|    2|
|refunded|    2|
+--------+-----+
```

Bottom up: `LocalTableScan` reads the input, `Generate explode(split(...))` is the map, `partial_count` is the combiner, `Exchange hashpartitioning(word, 4)` is the shuffle with R = 4 (Spark calls a shuffle an exchange), and the top `count(1)` is the reduce. The `#6` and `plan_id` numbers vary between runs.

refs.title: Resilient Distributed Datasets (Zaharia et al., NSDI 2012)

analogy: Think of the post. Each local post office (a map task) collects letters and bundles them by destination city (partitioning). Trucks carry every city's bundles from every office to that city's sorting center (the shuffle). Each center sorts by street and delivers (reduce). A local office that ties all its letters for one address into a single bundle is a combiner. If an office burns down before its trucks leave, the letters are lost, and someone has to collect them again from the senders. The analogy breaks there: real letters exist once, while MapReduce can re-run the map task because the input block still has copies on other machines.
in_your_world: You already run a shuffle every day: Kafka. The producer picks a partition for each record by hashing its key modulo the partition count. So every event for one card lands in one partition, and one consumer sees all of them in order. That is MapReduce's partitioning function, used for streaming. The same rule explains a Kafka surprise you may have met: add partitions to a topic and keys move, because hash mod R changes when R changes. MapReduce avoided that by fixing R for the life of a job. And if your settlement consumer keeps per-merchant totals in memory and flushes them every minute instead of writing a row per event, you have written a combiner.
mistake: The common mistake is treating the combiner as a free speed-up that can't change results. It can. Hadoop may run a combiner zero, one or several times on a map task's output, so the job must give the same answer however many times it runs. Sum, count and max pass that test. Average, "first status seen", and anything that counts its own calls fail it, and the failure is a wrong number, not an error. Make the combiner's output the same shape as its input, such as `(sum, count)` pairs, and finish the arithmetic in reduce.

compare.title: Word count in Hadoop MapReduce and in Spark

a.label: Hadoop MapReduce (Java)
a.title: TokenMapper.java and SumReducer.java

b.label: Spark DataFrame (Kotlin)
b.title: the same job
b.src:
val counts = lines
    .select(explode(split(lower(col("value")), "[^a-z]+")).alias("word"))
    .where(col("word").notEqual(""))
    .groupBy("word")
    .count()    // partial count per partition, shuffle by word, final count

counts.write().parquet("out/word_counts")

compare.note: The Hadoop version spells out the map and reduce functions, and you choose the combiner yourself. The Spark version says what you want, a count per word, and Spark's planner picks the same physical steps: a partial count on each partition, a hash shuffle by word, a final count. The bigger difference is between jobs. Two chained Hadoop jobs talk through files in HDFS. Two Spark steps in one plan pass data along without writing it to the distributed file system. Only the shuffle, and spills when memory runs short, touch local disk.

worked.title: Average ticket size per merchant, with a combiner that stays correct

steps.say: Finance wants the average authorization amount per merchant across 3 billion rows. The shuffle is huge, so you want a combiner. The tempting one averages each map task's amounts. Check it on three numbers before trusting it.

The fix is to carry what an average is made of. A partial result is a sum and a count, and adding two partials gives another partial. Addition is associative and commutative, so the framework may combine in any order, any number of times.
Check it on the same numbers. Task 1 combines to `(4,000, 2)`, task 2 to `(10,000, 1)`. The reducer adds them and divides once.
steps.code:
// 3. same input, right answer
val result = reduce(listOf(SumCount(4_000, 2), SumCount(10_000, 1)))   // 14,000 / 3 = 4,666.67

steps.say: Spark plans `avg` this way on its own. In its physical plan the step before the shuffle is `partial_avg`, which keeps a sum and a count per partition, and the step after it finishes the division.
steps.code:
// 4. in Spark: HashAggregate(partial_avg) -> Exchange hashpartitioning(merchant_id) -> HashAggregate(avg)
payments.groupBy("merchant_id").agg(avg("amount_cents"))

lab.title: MapReduce word count by hand, then in Spark
steps: Run the tests. All eleven fail. `MapReduceJob.run` at the bottom of `MapReduce.kt` is already written: it calls the pieces you are about to write, in order. Read it first.
Write `WordCount.map`, `combine` and `reduce`. Follow the rule in the KDoc exactly: lowercase first, then split on anything outside a to z.
Write `HashPartitioner.partition` with Hadoop's formula. One test feeds it `polygenelubricants`, whose `hashCode()` is `Int.MIN_VALUE`.
Write `Shuffle.shuffle`: route every pair to its bucket, count records and bytes (UTF-8 key length plus 4), then sort each bucket by key.
Run the tests. The job and combiner tests run your pieces together on 20,000 generated lines and compare against a plain `groupingBy`.
Write `SparkWordCount.count` with the DataFrame API and run all eleven tests. The last one reads Spark's physical plan and looks for your combiner and your shuffle in it.
hints: `line.lowercase().split(Regex("[^a-z]+"))` leaves an empty string when the line starts with a separator. Filter it out.
Kotlin's bitwise AND is the infix function `and`: `(key.hashCode() and Int.MAX_VALUE) % reducers`. `Math.abs(Int.MIN_VALUE)` is still negative.
`pairs.groupingBy { it.key }.fold(0) { acc, kv -> acc + kv.value }` sums per key in one pass.

For Spark: `explode(split(lower(col("value")), "[^a-z]+"))`, then `.where(col("word").notEqual(""))` and `.groupBy("word").count()`. Kotlin lets you call a Java method named `plus` as `+`, but `multiply` and `equalTo` stay method calls.

drill.title: Write the partitioner and the shuffle loop
drill.prompt: From memory, write `partition(key, reducers)` and the loop at the heart of `shuffle`: route each pair from each map task to its bucket and count the bytes moved. Then say in one sentence why Hadoop clears the sign bit instead of calling `Math.abs`.

recap: HDFS split files into 128 MB blocks, stored three times across DataNodes, with one NameNode holding the map of where every block lives.
MapReduce runs map, then a shuffle that partitions pairs by hash(key) mod R, writes them to local disk and lets each reducer fetch and sort its keys, then reduce.
A combiner pre-aggregates on the map side. It is only safe for associative and commutative work; for averages, carry `(sum, count)`.
Failures are handled by re-running deterministic tasks, including finished map tasks whose output died with their machine.
MapReduce lost because every job went through disk and HDFS. Its ideas live on as Spark's input partitions, `Exchange`, partial aggregates and shuffle files.

quiz.q: A MapReduce job has 4 reducers. The key `merchant-17` appears in the output of 200 of its 1,000 map tasks. How many reducers receive values for `merchant-17`?
quiz.why: The partitioner maps a key to one reducer, the same one from every map task, so all 200 tasks send `merchant-17` to one place. That is what lets a single reduce call see every value for the key. Four would mean the key was spread out and needed a second merge step.

quiz.q: A worker dies after its map task finished, but before the reducers fetched that task's output. What does MapReduce do?
options: Nothing: map output is replicated in HDFS
Re-runs the map task on another machine that holds a copy of the input block
Fails the whole job
Tells the reducers to skip that block
quiz.why: Map output lives on the map machine's local disk, not in HDFS, so it died with the machine. The input block still has copies elsewhere, and map is deterministic, so running it again gives the same output. Finished reduce output is the part that sits in HDFS.

quiz.q: Which job can safely reuse its reducer as the combiner?
options: Average transaction amount per merchant
Median latency per endpoint
The first status each payment reached
The largest single transaction per card
quiz.why: Max is associative and commutative, so taking the max of per-task maxes gives the true max, however many times the combiner runs. An average of averages is wrong when tasks see different row counts, a median can't be built from medians, and "first" depends on the order data arrives.

quiz.q: A Spark plan shows `HashAggregate(keys=[word], functions=[partial_count(1)])` just below `Exchange hashpartitioning(word, 200)`. What is `partial_count` doing?
options: Sampling rows to pick partition boundaries
Counting the files the scan will read
Counting each word within one partition before the shuffle, like a combiner
Checking that the shuffle lost no rows
quiz.why: The partial aggregate runs on each input partition before data moves, so each partition sends one row per distinct word instead of one per occurrence. The `Exchange` above it is the shuffle, and the final `count` above that is the reduce.

quiz.q: From the previous lesson: 1,000 map tasks each read one 128 MiB block at 100 MB/s, spread over 250 machines. Ignoring startup, about how long does the map phase take?
options: About 1.3 seconds
About 5.4 seconds
About 22 minutes
About 2 minutes
quiz.why: 1,000 tasks on 250 machines is 4 blocks for each machine. One block is 134,217,728 bytes, 1.34 s at 100 MB/s, so four take about 5.4 s. 1.3 s is a single block, and 22 minutes is one machine reading all 1,000 blocks.

flashcards.front: HDFS defaults for block size and replication?
flashcards.back: 128 MB blocks (`dfs.blocksize`) and 3 copies (`dfs.replication`). GFS used 64 MB chunks.

flashcards.front: What does the HDFS NameNode store?
flashcards.back: Only metadata: which blocks make up each file and which DataNodes hold each block. File data flows directly between clients and DataNodes.

flashcards.front: Why are finished map tasks re-run when their machine dies?
flashcards.back: Map output sits on the map machine's local disk, so it is lost with the machine. Reduce output is in HDFS, so finished reduce tasks are not re-run.
When the operation is associative and commutative (sum, count, min, max), so the answer doesn't depend on how many times or in what grouping it runs.

flashcards.front: Where does the combiner show up in a Spark physical plan?
flashcards.back: As a partial aggregate (`partial_count`, `partial_sum`, `partial_avg`) in a `HashAggregate` below the `Exchange`.

terms.plain: A large fixed-size piece of a file (128 MB in HDFS), stored and replicated as a unit.
The HDFS server that keeps the file-to-block map and where each block's copies live.
An HDFS server that stores blocks as files on its local disks and serves them to clients.
Running a task on a machine that already stores its input, so the data doesn't cross the network.
The function that picks which reducer owns a key, usually hash(key) mod R.
Moving map output across the network so every value for a key reaches that key's reducer, then sorting it.
Reduce logic run on one map task's output before the shuffle, to send fewer records.
The recorded chain of transformations that produced a dataset, which Spark uses to recompute lost partitions.

explain_back.prompt: A colleague says: "Spark replaced MapReduce because Spark runs in memory and never writes to disk." Explain what is right and what is wrong in that sentence, using the shuffle.
explain_back.answer: The right part: MapReduce wrote every job's output to HDFS, three copies, and a pipeline of jobs or an iterative algorithm paid that cost again and again. Spark keeps intermediate data in memory between steps of one plan and rebuilds lost partitions from lineage instead of replicating them. The wrong part is "never writes to disk". A shuffle still works like MapReduce's: the map side partitions its output by hash of the key and writes shuffle files to local disk, and the reduce side fetches them over the network. Spark's own guide says a shuffle generates many intermediate files on disk. So the shuffle is still the expensive step, and fewer or smaller shuffles is still how you make a Spark job faster.

deeper.body:
The MapReduce paper spends a page on stragglers, the slow tasks at the end of a job. A machine with a bad disk, or one shared with other work, can run a task many times slower than its peers, and the job waits for it. Google's fix was **backup tasks**: near the end of a job, the master starts a second copy of every task still running and takes whichever copy finishes first. The paper reports that its 1 TB sort took 44% longer with backup tasks turned off.

This only works because tasks are deterministic and their output is committed atomically. A reduce task writes to a temporary file and renames it to its final name when done; if two copies finish, the file system's atomic rename keeps exactly one.

Spark has the same idea under the name **speculative execution**. It is off by default (`spark.speculation=false`). When you turn it on, Spark considers re-launching a task that runs more than `spark.speculation.multiplier` times slower than the median task of its stage (3 by default). It is worth trying on clusters with noisy neighbours. It is useless when the slow task is slow because of its data: if one key holds a third of all rows, a copy of that task is just as slow. That problem is skew, and lesson 7 of this track handles it.
